title: CAN TECHNOLOGY BE USED TO STRENGTHEN HOLINESS?
paragraphs: CAN TECHNOLOGY BE USED TO STRENGTHEN HOLINESS?
The screen that has helped distract a generation from God may also become one of the places where a surrendered generation learns to seek Him again.
There is something strangely revealing about the glow of a phone in a dark room.
Nobody else is watching.
Nobody knows what you searched.
Nobody sees what you deleted.
Nobody hears what you listened to through your headphones.
Nobody knows whether you opened Scripture or pornography, worship or gossip, prayer or another hour of mindless scrolling.
Nobody knows.
Except God.
And perhaps that is where this conversation about technology and holiness really needs to begin.
Not with artificial intelligence.
Not with smartphones.
Not with algorithms.
Not with whether Christians should delete social media, install another Bible app, throw away their televisions, or retreat from the digital world entirely.
It begins with the heart.
Because technology has accomplished something remarkable: it has placed enormous power within inches of the human soul.
With the same device, you can read the Gospel of John or feed an addiction.
You can encourage somebody contemplating giving up or publicly humiliate someone you have never met.
You can listen to Scripture while driving to work or spend the journey poisoning your heart with envy.
You can send money to a missionary.
You can betray your marriage.
You can learn theology.
You can spread a lie.
You can pray with someone thousands of miles away.
You can secretly become somebody you would be ashamed for your family to meet.
Same screen.
Same hands.
Different master.
And that is why asking, “Is technology good or evil?” may be the wrong question.
A more uncomfortable question is:
What is technology revealing about who is ruling me?
Jesus said something centuries before smartphones that sounds terrifyingly contemporary:
“The lamp of the body is the eye.”
Matthew 6:22.
What enters through your eyes matters.
What repeatedly receives your attention matters.
What you rehearse in secret matters.
And Scripture’s call to holiness was never merely about looking respectable when other Christians were watching.
The apostle Peter writes:
1 Peter 1:15–16, KJV.
Behind Peter’s words stands an ancient command from Leviticus. In Hebrew:
קְדֹשִׁים תִּהְיוּ כִּי קָדוֹשׁ אֲנִי
Qedoshim tihyu, ki qadosh ani.
“You shall be holy, for I am holy.”
Holiness is not Christian cosmetic surgery.
It is not learning how to appear religious.
The Hebrew idea of קָדוֹשׁ — qadosh carries the sense of being holy, set apart, belonging to God.
And when the New Testament speaks of holiness, it uses words from the same spiritual world of consecration. Peter says:
ἅγιοι γενήθητε
hagioi genēthēte—
“become holy.”
That changes the question completely.
The question is no longer simply, “Can I use this?”
The question becomes:
“Can I use this while belonging completely to Jesus?”
Because holiness reaches your browser history.
Holiness reaches your private messages.
Holiness reaches the videos you watch after everyone goes to sleep.
Holiness reaches the comment you are about to type while angry.
Holiness reaches the photographs you keep returning to.
Holiness reaches your playlists.
Holiness reaches your search history.
Holiness reaches what you laugh at.
Holiness reaches what you secretly wish would appear next.
And suddenly the most dangerous thing about your phone may not be what technology can do.
It may be what technology can expose about you.
Paul wrote:
“All things are lawful for me, but all things are not expedient… I will not be brought under the power of any.”
1 Corinthians 6:12, KJV.
Read that last sentence again.
“I will not be brought under the power of any.”
That sounds almost prophetic in an age engineered around attention.
One more notification.
One more reel.
One more video.
One more refresh.
One more argument.
One more image.
One more purchase.
One more scroll before prayer.
Then prayer never happens.
You told yourself you were checking something for five minutes.
Forty-seven minutes disappeared.
The Bible remained unopened.
The person beside you remained unnoticed.
Your exhausted soul remained unfed.
And somehow you still felt hungry enough to keep scrolling.
Technology can give the human mind almost endless stimulation while leaving the human spirit starving.
But Christianity does not teach that holiness is achieved merely by throwing away objects.
Jesus goes deeper.
He goes after the throne.
Because if you destroy your smartphone while keeping an unsurrendered heart, the heart will eventually find another idol.
The problem is not ultimately silicon.
The problem is sin.
Jesus said:
“For from within, out of the heart of men, proceed evil thoughts, adulteries, fornications, murders…”
Mark 7:21, KJV.
That means your phone did not invent lust.
The internet did not invent pride.
Social media did not invent envy.
Algorithms did not invent greed.
Technology can amplify them, monetize them, normalize them, personalize them, and deliver temptations with unprecedented speed.
But sin was already inside the human heart.
And that matters because Christianity offers something far greater than digital minimalism.
Jesus did not die merely to make you use your phone less.
He died to reconcile sinners to God.
The Gospel is not:
Become disciplined enough and maybe God will accept you.
The Gospel is that sinners who could never cleanse themselves are offered forgiveness and reconciliation through Jesus Christ.
Paul says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
Romans 5:8, KJV.
While we were sinners.
Not after the browser history became respectable.
Not after the addiction disappeared.
Not after you finally became disciplined.
Not after you managed thirty consecutive mornings of devotion.
While we were sinners.
Christ died for us.
That does not make sin harmless.
It makes grace astonishing.
Maybe your digital life has become a place of shame.
Maybe there are things you have watched that you wish you could erase from your memory.
Maybe technology helped facilitate an affair.
Maybe pornography has become the secret prison behind your Christian smile.
Maybe comparison has quietly destroyed your gratitude.
Maybe you know everything happening in everybody else's life but cannot remember the last time you sat silently before God.
Maybe you post Bible verses publicly while privately becoming someone you barely recognize.
And perhaps the hardest sentence you need to hear is this:
Jesus already knows.
Not the edited version.
Not the Sunday version.
Not the version you would confess if you could control everybody’s reaction.
Everything.
And still the invitation of the Gospel is not, “Hide better.”
It is:
Come into the light.
John writes:
1 John 1:7, KJV.
That is where technology can begin to change roles.
The device that once helped you hide can become a tool that helps you walk toward the light.
No, an app cannot sanctify you.
An algorithm cannot regenerate you.
Artificial intelligence cannot give you the Holy Spirit.
A notification cannot produce repentance.
A digital Bible cannot save you merely because it occupies storage on your phone.
Only Christ saves.
Only the Holy Spirit transforms.
Only the Word of God possesses the authority of God’s Word.
Technology is a servant.
Never the Savior.
But servants can be useful when they remain under the authority of the King.
Imagine opening your phone tomorrow morning and seeing Scripture before social media.
Imagine setting reminders not merely for meetings but for prayer.
Imagine allowing technology to remind you to pray for your spouse, your children, your enemies, your church, and people who do not yet know Christ.
Imagine listening to Scripture during the commute that used to disappear into endless scrolling.
Imagine replacing one stream of temptation with sermons, worship, biblical teaching, and Christian books that deepen your understanding of Jesus.
Imagine using accountability software because you finally decided secrecy was costing too much.
Imagine removing an app—not because apps are inherently sinful, but because Jesus matters more to you than keeping something that repeatedly drags your heart away from Him.
That is not legalism.
That can be wisdom.
Jesus uses intentionally severe imagery when teaching about temptation:
“And if thy right hand offend thee, cut it off, and cast it from thee…”
Matthew 5:30, KJV.
Jesus is not commanding bodily mutilation. His shocking imagery communicates the seriousness with which disciples should deal with sin.
Some of us keep asking God for victory while preserving immediate access to the thing repeatedly defeating us.
We pray:
“Lord, deliver me.”
Then keep the door unlocked.
Keep the account active.
Keep the secret folder.
Keep following the person.
Keep the private conversation.
Keep the app.
Keep the midnight habit.
Keep saying, “I can handle it.”
Perhaps holiness sometimes looks surprisingly ordinary.
Delete.
Unfollow.
Block.
Turn it off.
Move the phone out of the bedroom.
Give somebody accountability.
Stop pretending.
Confess.
Run.
Not because these actions purchase righteousness before God, but because someone who belongs to Christ should not casually furnish a room for the sin Christ calls us to forsake.
Paul told Timothy:
“Flee also youthful lusts: but follow righteousness, faith, charity, peace…”
2 Timothy 2:22, KJV.
Notice the movement.
Flee.
Then:
Follow.
Christian holiness is not merely removing darkness.
It is pursuing Christ.
This is where technology becomes interesting.
Because the same architecture that forms habits around distraction can, when deliberately subordinated to godly purposes, support habits that point us toward what is good.
You can make temptation harder to access.
You can make Scripture easier to access.
You can schedule silence.
You can create boundaries.
You can curate what repeatedly enters your mind.

You can use digital tools to study biblical languages, compare faithful translations, listen to Scripture, memorize passages, join prayer communities, support ministries, receive devotionals, access Christian books, and remain connected to believers when isolation would otherwise swallow you.
But never confuse the scaffolding with the building.
A Bible notification is not Bible meditation.
Saving a sermon is not obeying it.
Sharing a Christian post is not discipleship.
Following a Christian page is not following Jesus.
We should never ask technology to do what only God can do.
That distinction matters even more as artificial intelligence becomes woven into daily life.
AI can help organize information.
It can assist study.
It can explain vocabulary.
It can generate questions.
It can help locate passages.
It can help believers think through ideas.
But Christians must remain discerning.
An AI system can be wrong.
It can misunderstand Scripture.
It can confidently produce inaccurate claims.
It does not possess divine inspiration simply because it speaks fluently about God.
So test what you receive.
Return to Scripture.
Read passages in context.
Compare responsible translations.
Learn from faithful teachers.
Be like the Bereans, who received teaching eagerly but still searched the Scriptures to determine whether those things were true.
Acts 17:11 gives us a remarkably relevant principle for the digital age:
Do not outsource discernment.
Not to influencers.
Not to pastors.
Not to algorithms.
Not to artificial intelligence.
Not even to Gospel Warrior.
Bring teaching back to Scripture.
Because technology becomes spiritually dangerous whenever convenience begins replacing discernment.
And perhaps this is the deeper battle happening inside your pocket every day.
Your phone is competing for something extraordinarily precious.
Your attention.
And attention eventually becomes affection.
What you repeatedly behold can shape what you increasingly desire.
Paul therefore gives Christians a radically different algorithm:

“Whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report… think on these things.”
Philippians 4:8, KJV.
Imagine treating that verse as a filter for your digital life.
Is this true?
Is this pure?
Is this feeding hatred?
Is this awakening lust?
Is this cultivating envy?
Is this making me more compassionate?
Is this making sin look entertaining?
Is this strengthening gratitude?
Is this helping me love Jesus?
Is this consuming time God has entrusted to me while giving almost nothing of lasting value in return?
Those questions can hurt.
Because sometimes we do not need another app.
We need repentance.
Sometimes the most spiritually productive thing your phone can do is remain face down.
Sometimes holiness sounds like silence.
Sometimes worship begins when the screen goes dark.
Sometimes the notification can wait because your child is speaking.
Sometimes the message can wait because your spouse needs your eyes.
Sometimes the world can continue without knowing your opinion.
Sometimes you need to sit before God without photographing it, posting it, measuring it, monetizing it, or telling anybody it happened.
Just you.
Your Bible.
Your weakness.
Your Father.
And perhaps tears nobody online will ever see.
Jesus Himself repeatedly withdrew to pray.
If the sinless Son of God deliberately withdrew from crowds, how much more should distracted people recognize their need for solitude with God?
Technology can strengthen practices that support holiness.
But technology cannot replace the secret place.
And there is another side of this conversation Christians cannot ignore.
Your technology is not only a doorway through which content reaches you.
It is a doorway through which you reach others.
There is somebody scrolling tonight who believes God could never forgive what they have done.
Somebody whose marriage is collapsing.
Somebody hiding an addiction.
Somebody sitting in a hospital hallway.
Somebody grieving.
Somebody questioning whether Christianity is real.
Somebody who has not prayed in twenty years.
Somebody who thinks their scandal is the final chapter.
And then your share appears.
Not because Facebook is holy.
Not because an algorithm is evangelism.
But because a believer decided that a tool normally used for self-promotion could also be used to point toward Jesus.
Paul asked:
“And how shall they hear without a preacher?”
Romans 10:14, KJV.
For most of Christian history, believers could scarcely imagine communicating instantly with thousands of people across nations.
We can.
That privilege should sober us.
The Gospel entrusted to the church is infinitely more important than our personal brands.
Your profile can become another place where truth is spoken.
Your comment can become encouragement.
Your message can become an invitation.
Your share can place Scripture before someone you could never reach physically.
Your technology can become an instrument of mercy.
But there is a warning even here.
You can share Jesus without actually walking with Jesus.
You can build an audience while neglecting your soul.
You can become obsessed with engagement while forgetting obedience.
You can publicly defend biblical morality while privately starving your relationship with God.
Jesus is not impressed by Christian visibility without Christian faithfulness.
Holiness still begins where applause cannot reach you.
So perhaps the question is not merely whether technology can strengthen holiness.
Yes, technology can support habits, boundaries, learning, accountability, fellowship, evangelism, and access to Scripture that may help believers pursue lives of obedience.
But technology itself cannot make anyone holy.

Holiness is the work of God in people who have been united to Christ, called to repentance, indwelt and transformed by the Holy Spirit, shaped by Scripture, and increasingly taught to say no to sin and yes to righteousness.
Technology can assist the disciple.
It cannot become the Master.
And maybe tonight your first act of digital discipleship is not downloading anything.
Maybe it is confession.
“Jesus, this has been mastering me.”
“This has been feeding my lust.”
“This has been stealing my attention.”
“This has been poisoning my contentment.”
“This has become more important to me than Your presence.”
“This is where I keep hiding.”
“This is what I am afraid to surrender.”
Then bring it into the light.
Not because Christ is waiting to humiliate you.
Because Christ died for sinners.
There is a cross standing between your scandal and your final sentence.
There is an empty tomb declaring that sin and death do not get the last word over those who belong to Jesus.
There is grace for the ashamed.
Forgiveness for the repentant.
Power for the weak.
Restoration for the fallen.
A new direction for the person who thought they had gone too far.
That is our heartbeat at Gospel Warrior:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling darkness light.
Not by lowering the holiness of God until everybody feels comfortable.

Jesus rewrites lives by meeting sinners with truth and grace, calling us to repentance, forgiving those who come to Him, and transforming people who once lived for themselves into people increasingly surrendered to Him.
So use the technology.
But do not worship it.
Use the Bible app.
Then obey the Bible.
Use the reminder.
Then pray.
Use the blocker.
Then pursue purity.
Use the sermon.
Then test it against Scripture.
Use AI carefully.
Then practice discernment.
Use social media.
Then refuse to let social media use you.
And if necessary, shut the entire thing down for a while and rediscover what your soul sounds like when the noise finally stops.
Be honest.
Somebody reading silently may need evidence that surrender is possible and that God is still restoring people.
Not because saving a post makes anyone holy.
Come back when the screen begins becoming your master again.
And think of one person right now.
Not fifty.
One.
The friend whose faith is cooling.
The teenager being discipled more aggressively by an algorithm than by Christians.
The husband hiding something.
The wife exhausted by comparison.
The believer who keeps falling into pornography.
The seeker who assumes Christianity is only rules and condemnation.
The person whose private scandal has convinced them grace could never reach them.
Or send this privately.
We glorify God through faith in Christ expressed in love and obedience, not through supporting a page.

But if this ministry is faithfully pointing people toward Jesus, sharing its biblical content is one practical way you can help put Gospel truth in front of people who might otherwise never encounter it.
That matters.
Supporting faithful Gospel work can itself become an act of Christian stewardship when the motive is love for Christ rather than pressure, recognition, or spiritual bargaining.
It does not.
Not because giving money makes you more holy.
It cannot.
And certainly not because anyone must financially support Gospel Warrior in order to glorify God.
Scripture would not permit us to make that claim.
And beyond products, the deeper reason to stay close is discipleship.
Read.
Study.
Test everything against Scripture.
Grow.
Share what strengthens you.
Bring somebody else with you.
Deeper than a follow.
Deeper than a share.
Deeper than Christian content.
He calls us to follow Him.
So when you put this article down and your thumb reaches instinctively toward the next distraction, remember the question that began all of this:
Who is ruling me?
Your screen may know your habits.
Your algorithm may predict your desires.
Your browser may remember your history.
But none of them gets to write your ending.
Your history may live in the cloud, but your future belongs in the hands of the Christ who still turns hidden scandals into testimonies of grace.
